A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TimeSuite/VideoChat-T work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and rendered figures, support reliable comparison despite appendix reorganization and added experiments.

before.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original temporal-grounding and video-QA evaluations, component and data ablations, and qualitative results.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds computational measurements, transfer experiments, diagnostic ablations and reasoning-failure examples.

M1.justification: The specified Token Shuffle, TAPE, Temporal Grounded Caption and grounded-tuning procedure remain unchanged, including Algorithm 1. Appendix F.4 applies the existing TimeSuite to LLaVA-OneVision without specifying a new method component or revised procedure.

E1.justification: V2 newly evaluates on MLVU in the LLaVA-OneVision transfer experiment (Table 14); v1 only cited this benchmark. Existing evaluation datasets and the default TimePro task coverage are retained, making this a limited coverage extension.

E2.justification: V2 adds Qwen2-VL and LLaVA-OneVision as evaluated comparators in Table 7 across five existing benchmarks and computational efficiency. This substantially broadens the comparative assessment beyond v1's evaluated methods, while retaining the original comparator sets.

E3.justification: New experimental designs include 128-frame FLOP measurements and single-A100 inference timing, initialization and full-training-data controls, TimeChat fine-tuning on matched data, and alternative data sizes and mixtures (Tables 7 and 12–17). These are additional protocols; the original three-epoch training schedule and default hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component, frame-count and STAR ablations, v2 investigates MVBench degradation, architecture versus training-data contributions, transfer to LLaVA-OneVision, data pruning and temporal/non-temporal data mixtures. Figure 9 additionally examines two complex-reasoning failures. These additions substantially expand diagnostic and robustness evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, uncertainty intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's additional experiments continue the existing point-score reporting practice.

E6.justification: Original benchmark and ablation values are retained. New results include 35.5 T FLOPs and 0.63-second inference in Table 7, 62.9 MVBench accuracy under full-data fine-tuning in Table 12, and MLVU scores of 64.7 versus 69.4 for baseline versus transferred LLaVA-OneVision in Table 14. Additional data-ablation and failure-case outcomes substantially expand results; these do not represent improvements to the unchanged original evaluation setting.

T1.justification: The token-concatenation definitions and dimensional relationships are unchanged. Neither version adds formal assumptions, theorems or proofs; the new explanatory discussions are qualitative.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same architectural, dataset and Temporal Grounded Caption contributions and the same long-video QA and grounding claims, including the reported 5.6- and 6.8-point gains. The appendix additions provide further evidence without redefining these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of MVBench degradation through architectural distribution mismatch and training-data differences, and discusses data diversity and complementarity (F.2 and G.2–G.3). Appendix C introduces accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs and a feature-redundancy hypothesis. H.2 explicitly identifies failures of motivational and causal reasoning despite correct timestamps, attributing them to limited multi-step reasoning data.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-and-dataset availability statement and repository link, the single-A100 inference setup, and previously undocumented data-curation counts in F.5. Existing TAPE code and default hyperparameters are retained. The newly documented 615K precursor configuration does not replace v1's default: both PDFs use 349K TimePro examples.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen2-VL and the temporal grounding bridge work by Wang et al. Related-work edits and the new efficiency comparison extend positioning, while the central relationship to general video MLLMs and grounding-specialized methods remains intact.

P1.justification: The main narrative remains largely unchanged. V2 makes localized related-work edits, replaces numbered related-work subsections with paragraph headings, adds conference/contact and acknowledgment text, and reorganizes the appendices. The original discussion becomes G.1, and the retained case study moves to Appendix H.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual presentation with the efficiency/performance Table 7, diagnostic, transfer and data-comparison Tables 12–17, and failure-case Figure 9. Existing Figures 6–8 are relocated to Appendix H, and original appendix tables are renumbered. Main-text figures and table structures are largely preserved.

improvement.justification: V1's general adaptation claim was evaluated on one base model; v2 adds LLaVA-OneVision transfer and matched-data, initialization and data-composition controls (Tables 12–17), addressing important gaps in generality and performance attribution. Measured efficiency tradeoffs and explicit reasoning failures also make applicability substantially clearer. Statistical uncertainty and some experimental details remain unreported, but the added evidence materially strengthens the paper.
